title: Detection of SARS-CoV-2 and a possible variant in shelter cats
authors: Okwumabua O, Bradley-Siemens N, Cruz C, Chittick L, Thompson M
abstract: Researchers tested conjunctival, pharyngeal, and serum samples from 350 cats housed in an animal shelter, collected between July and December 2020, for SARS-CoV-2 using rRT-PCR targeting the N1 and N2 genes plus a surrogate virus neutralization test. Results showed that 203 (58%) swab samples were negative (N1 and N2 not detected), 2 (0.6%) were positive (N1 and N2 detected) and 145 (41%) were inconclusive (only N1 detected). Analysis revealed base-pair deletions and substitutions in the N2 probe binding region of the feline samples RNA extracts in comparison with the positive control. When using a redesigned cat-derived probe, 123 of 127 (96.9%) of the N2 negative samples returned positive results. The study concludes that cats can harbor the virus and serve as a potential source for virus spread, and suggests cats may carry a yet-to-be-described virus that is somewhat related to SARS-CoV-2.

mcqs.q: In a shelter-based SARS-CoV-2 surveillance study using rRT-PCR, what proportion of cat swab samples were inconclusive (N1 detected only, N2 not detected)?
mcqs.e: 203 of 350 samples (58%) were fully negative; 2 (0.6%) fully positive; 145 (41%) were inconclusive with only N1 detected. The high inconclusive rate prompted redesign of the N2 probe.

mcqs.q: The high rate of inconclusive N2 results in shelter cats tested for SARS-CoV-2 was best explained by which finding?
o: Inadequate sample collection technique
Base-pair deletions and substitutions in the N2 probe binding region of feline RNA extracts
Low viral load below assay detection limit
Cross-reactivity with feline coronavirus
mcqs.e: The study found base-pair deletions and substitutions in the N2 probe binding region of the feline samples compared with the positive control, reducing N2 assay sensitivity in this species.

mcqs.q: What was the key public health implication of this shelter cat SARS-CoV-2 study?
o: Shelter cats are not susceptible to SARS-CoV-2
Standard human PCR assays are fully reliable for feline SARS-CoV-2 detection
Cats can harbor SARS-CoV-2 and may carry a related novel virus, warranting vigilance in shelter settings
SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence in shelter cats exceeded 90%
mcqs.e: The authors concluded that cats can harbor the virus and serve as a potential source for spread, and that the feline samples may represent a yet-to-be-described related virus—both findings relevant to shelter infection control.

title: A prospective study of mental wellbeing, quality of life, human-animal attachment, and grief among foster caregivers at animal shelters
authors: Powell L, Ackerman R, Reinhard CL, Serpell J, Watson B
abstract: This longitudinal study examined 131 foster caregivers from five U.S. animal shelters between March 2022 and 2023. Participants completed three online surveys at baseline, during fostering, and post-placement. Key findings: positive affect decreased significantly after foster animals departed (p<0.01), particularly among dog caregivers. Negative affect remained stable throughout. Dog caregivers reported greater emotional and social/physical quality-of-life benefits than cat caregivers. Foster caregivers demonstrated secure attachment patterns with low anxious and avoidant attachment scores. Most caregivers (86%) indicated likelihood of future fostering participation. Caregivers reported experiencing both anticipatory and ambiguous grief upon animal departure. The researchers concluded that while fostering at animal shelters may serve as a One Health intervention by offering companionship, affection, and emotional support, mental wellbeing improvements were not evident, warranting caution about positioning foster care as a mental health promotion strategy.

mcqs.q: In a longitudinal study of 131 shelter foster caregivers, which of the following changes in wellbeing was observed after the foster animal's departure?
o: Significant decrease in negative affect
Significant decrease in positive affect, particularly among dog caregivers
Significant improvement in mental wellbeing scores overall
No change in any wellbeing domain
mcqs.e: Positive affect decreased significantly (p<0.01) after foster animals left, especially among dog foster caregivers, while negative affect remained unchanged throughout.

mcqs.q: Based on findings from a prospective study of animal shelter foster caregivers, which conclusion about foster care as a One Health intervention is best supported?
o: Foster care reliably improves foster caregiver mental health and should be broadly promoted as a wellbeing tool
Foster care provided companionship benefits but did not produce measurable mental wellbeing improvements, so caution is warranted
Foster care caused significant psychological harm and increased negative affect in caregivers
Foster care exclusively benefited cat caregivers over dog caregivers
mcqs.e: The authors concluded fostering offers companionship and emotional support but mental wellbeing improvements were not evident, warranting caution about promoting it as a mental health tool.

mcqs.q: What retention rate did shelter foster caregivers report at the end of a three-timepoint longitudinal wellbeing study?
mcqs.e: 86% of caregivers reported they were likely to provide foster care in the future, indicating strong retention despite the emotional challenges of animal departure.

title: Quantification of a shelter cat population: Trends in intake, length of stay and outcome data of cats in seven Dutch shelters between 2006 and 2021
authors: van der Leij WJR, Vernooij JCM, Vinke CM, Corbee RJ, Hesselink JW
abstract: Shelters utilize metrics for self-assessment to enhance animal population health and identify disease outbreak risk factors. However, broader metric applications are needed for benchmarking and developing best practices. This retrospective study analyzed data from seven Dutch shelters over 2006–2021, examining intake sources, outcomes, and length of stay for over 74,000 cats. Key findings demonstrate that feline intake decreased by 39% per 1,000 residents, while euthanasia cases declined approximately 50%. Length of stay showed reducing trends, and return-to-owner rates increased alongside the risk-based live release rate. The researchers conclude these metrics effectively monitor shelter management, animal health and welfare, and can measure progress both nationally and across Europe.

mcqs.q: In a retrospective analysis of seven Dutch animal shelters over 15 years (2006–2021), which outcome trend was observed for cats?
o: Intake increased by 39% per 1,000 residents while euthanasia increased
Intake decreased by 39% per 1,000 residents and euthanasia declined approximately 50%
Length of stay increased while live release rate decreased
Return-to-owner rates declined despite improved population management
mcqs.e: The study found intake fell 39% per 1,000 residents and euthanasia declined ~50% over the study period, alongside improving length-of-stay and return-to-owner metrics.

mcqs.q: Which statement best reflects the purpose of population-level shelter metrics such as those analyzed across seven Dutch shelters?
o: They are used exclusively to assess individual animal welfare during a single shelter stay
They enable shelter self-assessment, benchmarking across facilities, and monitoring progress in population health management
They primarily document disease incidence rather than outcome or length-of-stay trends
They are only applicable in high-intake open-admission municipal shelters
mcqs.e: The authors emphasized that these metrics serve self-assessment, benchmarking, and tracking of shelter management progress nationally and across Europe—beyond individual animal assessment.

title: Social mechanisms for integrating community cats into community governance in urban China
authors: Wu D, Gu J
abstract: The presence of unowned cats roaming urban spaces has generated considerable debate. This research examines how community cats become incorporated into neighborhood governance through resident interactions. Using participatory observation and interviews, the study applies a social capital framework examining norms, trust, and networks. The findings reveal that social norms and trust activate community social capital, creating a social network centered on community cat care. Notably, this network extends care beyond cats to encompass other community members. The researchers term this mechanism 'care extension.' The study concludes that this approach fosters neighborly bonds transcending ecological relationships, ultimately contributing to a compassionate and harmonious multi-species urban community.

mcqs.q: A qualitative study of community cat management in urban China found that community cat care networks operate through which social mechanism?
o: Formal government mandates enforcing TNR compliance
Social capital activation through norms and trust, creating care networks that extend to human community members
Financial incentives provided by municipal shelters to caretakers
Ecological monitoring programs linked to biodiversity conservation targets
mcqs.e: The study found that social norms and trust activated community social capital, forming networks centered on cat care that extended to broader community welfare—termed 'care extension' by the authors.

mcqs.q: According to a social capital framework analysis of urban community cat governance in China, which outcome was observed beyond cat care itself?
o: Significant reduction in stray cat population through TNR
Strengthened neighborly bonds and extension of care to other community members
Increased municipal shelter intake due to caregiver burnout
Reduced zoonotic disease transmission in managed colonies
mcqs.e: The 'care extension' mechanism described means that community cat care networks fostered human-to-human bonds and care, contributing to broader community cohesion.

title: Rethinking the Animal Shelter's Role in Free-Roaming Cat Management
authors: Hurley KF, Levy JK
abstract: This article examines three shelter-based strategies for managing free-roaming cats: removal through impoundment, sterilization with return to location of origin, and leaving cats in place with community referrals. The authors argue that traditional removal programs are ineffective at population control, noting that removal short of eradication may not only fail to decrease the population, it can magnify concerns. They present evidence that sterilization-and-return programs show promise for reducing shelter intake while improving cat welfare. The paper advocates for an evidence-based approach recognizing that most free-roaming cats remain in communities regardless of shelter intervention, and recommends individualized case management tailored to specific circumstances rather than standardized policies.

mcqs.q: According to a 2022 Frontiers in Veterinary Science analysis, why do traditional shelter removal programs for free-roaming cats often fail to achieve population control?
o: Removed cats are immediately replaced by immigration from surrounding areas, and removal short of eradication may magnify concerns
Shelter vaccination protocols are inadequate for returning cats
Community opposition prevents capture of sufficient numbers
Cats removed from colonies become aggressive and unadoptable
mcqs.e: Hurley and Levy argue that removal short of eradication may not only fail to decrease the population but can magnify concerns; most free-roaming cats remain in communities regardless of shelter removal.

mcqs.q: Which shelter-based strategy for free-roaming cat management did Hurley and Levy (2022) present as most promising for reducing shelter intake while improving cat welfare?
o: Impoundment followed by adoption or euthanasia
Sterilization with return to location of origin (Shelter-Neuter-Return / Return-to-Field)
Leaving all cats in place without intervention
Mass vaccination without sterilization
mcqs.e: The paper presents evidence that sterilization-and-return programs (RTF/SNR/CCP) show promise for reducing shelter intake while improving welfare, in contrast to traditional removal programs.

mcqs.q: What management approach do Hurley and Levy (2022) recommend for shelters dealing with free-roaming cats, given that most cats remain in communities regardless of intervention?
o: A single standardized national policy applied uniformly across all shelter types
Individualized case management tailored to specific circumstances rather than standardized policies
Mandatory euthanasia of all unadoptable free-roaming cats
Postponing action until TNR effectiveness is proven in controlled trials
mcqs.e: The authors call for individualized, evidence-based case management recognizing community context rather than rigid uniform policies.

title: COVID-19 associated reduction in elective spay-neuter surgeries for dogs and cats
authors: Guerios SD, Porcher TR, Clemmer G, Denagamage T, Levy JK
abstract: The study examined pandemic impacts on sterilization procedures using data from 212 clinics. Surgeries decreased 13% to 1,059,388 in 2020 compared to the 2019 baseline of approximately 1.2 million procedures. April 2020 experienced the steepest decline at negative 80%. By 2021, procedures partially recovered but remained 3% below the baseline year. The analysis projected that if similar patterns affected all U.S. spay-neuter providers, there could be a deficit of more than 2.7 million unperformed surgeries. The study emphasizes concerns about potential increases in unwanted litters and reversals in population control achievements, noting that as of August 2022, spay-neuter clinics had not yet returned to baseline productivity due to ongoing workforce shortages of veterinarians and staff.

mcqs.q: A 2022 analysis of 212 U.S. spay-neuter clinics found that elective surgeries declined by what percentage in April 2020 at the height of COVID-19 disruptions?
mcqs.e: April 2020 saw the steepest single-month decline at approximately 80%; the overall annual decline for 2020 was 13% compared to 2019.

mcqs.q: According to COVID-19 spay-neuter impact data from 212 clinics, what was the projected national deficit in sterilization surgeries if pandemic-level reductions affected all U.S. providers?
o: Approximately 500,000 surgeries
Approximately 1.2 million surgeries
More than 2.7 million surgeries
More than 5 million surgeries
mcqs.e: The authors projected a deficit of more than 2.7 million unperformed surgeries if similar reductions applied across all U.S. spay-neuter providers.

mcqs.q: What was the status of U.S. spay-neuter clinic productivity as of August 2022, according to this Frontiers in Veterinary Science study?
o: Fully recovered to pre-pandemic 2019 baseline levels
Exceeded 2019 baseline by 10% due to pent-up demand
Remained 3% below 2019 baseline due to ongoing workforce shortages
Remained more than 20% below 2019 levels
mcqs.e: By 2021 procedures recovered to 3% below baseline, and by August 2022 clinics had not yet returned to full productivity due to ongoing veterinarian and staff workforce shortages.

title: The Impact of Incorporating Multiple Best Practices on Live Outcomes for a Municipal Animal Shelter in Memphis, TN
authors: Kreisler RE, Pugh AA, Pemberton K, Pizano S
abstract: Modern shelters are encouraged to adopt best practices promoting animal life-saving. Memphis Animal Services implemented five strategies in 2017 and tracked their effects: managed strategic intake, pet owner safety nets, community cat return-to-field programs, transforming field services from enforcement to assistance, and streamlined adoption/transfer processes. For cats, the median live release rate increased from 35% to 92% post-intervention. The correlation between intake and euthanasia shifted from significant and very strong (r = 0.982) to non-significant (−0.165). For dogs, rates improved from 25% to 87%. Kitten euthanasia decreased dramatically from a median of 59% to 3% of kittens entering the shelter. Dog return-to-owner rates improved from 10% to 13%. The study demonstrates that implementation of these best practices accelerated progress toward a live release rate of at least 90%, particularly for cats, dramatically decreased kitten euthanasia, increased the return-to-owner rate for dogs, and severed the historical correlation between euthanasia and intake.

mcqs.q: After implementing five shelter best practices at Memphis Animal Services in 2017, the median live release rate for cats changed from approximately:
mcqs.e: Cat live release rates increased from 35% to 92%. The 25-to-87% figure applies to dogs; 59-to-3% is the kitten euthanasia change; 10-to-13% is the dog return-to-owner change.

mcqs.q: Which of the five best practices implemented at Memphis Animal Services directly addressed population management of free-roaming cats?
o: Managed strategic intake
Pet owner safety nets
Community cat return-to-field programs
Streamlined adoption/transfer processes
mcqs.e: Community cat return-to-field (RTF) programs—sterilizing, vaccinating, and returning healthy stray cats—directly addressed free-roaming cat population management and contributed to the dramatic improvement in cat live release rates.

mcqs.q: Before implementing shelter best practices, the correlation between intake numbers and euthanasia at Memphis Animal Services was described as:
o: Weak and non-significant (r = −0.165)
Moderate and positive (r = 0.50)
Significant and very strong (r = 0.982)
Absent; euthanasia was driven by disease status not intake
mcqs.e: Pre-intervention, intake and euthanasia were very strongly correlated (r = 0.982). Post-intervention, this correlation became non-significant (r = −0.165), showing that high intake no longer drove euthanasia.

title: Animal shelter management of feline leukemia virus and feline immunodeficiency virus infections in cats
authors: Dezubiria P, Amirian ES, Spera K, Crawford PC, Levy JK
abstract: This study examined feline retroviral management practices among 139 Florida animal shelters. The survey covered testing protocols, diagnostic techniques, and outcome options for cats with positive results. Key findings showed that 83% of shelters performed at least some testing, primarily using combination point-of-care devices for simultaneous FeLV antigen and FIV antibody screening. Testing selection varied by population: screening adoptable cats (108 shelters; 94%) was most common, while testing cats in trap-neuter-return programs was least common (18%). For positive cats, common outcomes included adoption (64%), transfer (54%), and euthanasia (43%). Euthanasia was more prevalent for FeLV-positive cats than FIV-positive ones, and more common in municipal shelters with lower live outcome rates. The authors concluded that while most shelters offered live outcome options, increased access to training and practical tools could enhance testing protocols and support better outcomes for this vulnerable population.

mcqs.q: In a survey of 139 Florida animal shelters, what percentage performed at least some FeLV/FIV testing, and what was the most common diagnostic method?
o: 65% performed testing, primarily using individual FeLV ELISA tests
83% performed testing, primarily using combination point-of-care devices for simultaneous FeLV antigen and FIV antibody screening
91% performed testing using PCR as the primary method
50% performed testing using IFA as the standard technique
mcqs.e: 83% of the 139 shelters performed some testing, and combination point-of-care devices screening for both FeLV antigen and FIV antibody simultaneously were the most common method.

mcqs.q: In Florida shelter retroviral management, testing of cats in TNR programs was least common compared to testing adoptable cats. Approximately what percentage of shelters tested TNR cats for FeLV/FIV?
mcqs.e: Only 18% of shelters tested cats in TNR programs, compared to 94% that tested adoptable cats. This reflects the different management pathway for TNR cats who return to the field.

mcqs.q: For FeLV- or FIV-positive cats in Florida shelters, which outcome was more likely to be used for FeLV-positive cats compared to FIV-positive cats?
o: Adoption
Transfer
Euthanasia
TNR return-to-field
mcqs.e: Euthanasia was more prevalent for FeLV-positive cats than FIV-positive cats, reflecting the more serious prognosis and greater infectivity concerns associated with FeLV.

title: Cross-sectional survey exploring current intake practices for dogs admitted to animal shelters in Texas: a descriptive study
authors: Cranford M, Bing A, Cisneros A, Carroll AD, Porter H, Stellato AC
abstract: The researchers examined shelter intake procedures in Texas through a survey of 64 shelter employees across 47 counties. Staff reported varying handling approaches based on dog demeanor—using treats and gentle techniques for calm animals, but escalating to muzzles and catch poles for aggressive dogs. Most participants asked about behavioral history during owner surrenders, particularly regarding aggression. After exams, approximately 45% housed dogs on adoption floors. The authors note that while many current practices align with stress-reduction recommendations, future research should provide evidence-based protocols to support dog welfare during intake procedures and handler safety.

mcqs.q: In a cross-sectional survey of Texas shelter intake practices, what percentage of shelters placed dogs on adoption floors directly after intake examination?
o: Approximately 15%
Approximately 30%
Approximately 45%
Approximately 75%
mcqs.e: Approximately 45% of surveyed shelter staff reported housing dogs on adoption floors after intake exams, illustrating variation in shelter intake-to-placement pathways.

mcqs.q: During owner surrender intake in Texas shelters, what behavioral information did most shelter staff prioritize collecting?
o: Vaccination history and parasite prevention records
Behavioral history, particularly regarding aggression
Microchip status and prior ownership duration
Nutritional and diet history
mcqs.e: Most participants asked about behavioral history during owner surrenders, with aggression history being of particular importance for making safe housing and handling decisions.

title: Effects of single- or pair-housing on the welfare of shelter dogs: Behavioral and physiological indicators
authors: Hecker G, Martineau K, Scheskie M, Hammerslough R, Feuerbacher EN
abstract: The researchers investigated whether housing shelter dogs in compatible pairs versus alone affects their wellbeing. They observed 61 dogs (30 single-housed; 31 pair-housed) over seven days, collecting daily behavioral videos and urine samples for cortisol:creatinine analysis. Results showed pair-housed dogs exhibited significantly fewer stress indicators including lip licking, whining, and ears back compared to solitary dogs. The pair-housed group demonstrated greater reductions in cortisol levels and had shorter adoption timeframes by approximately four days. The study found that well-matched pair-housing can have both proximate and ultimate welfare benefits for shelter dogs, with minimal aggression concerns and evidence of affiliative behaviors between compatible pairs.

mcqs.q: A controlled study comparing single- vs. pair-housing in 61 shelter dogs found that pair-housed dogs had which of the following outcomes compared to single-housed dogs?
o: Higher cortisol levels and longer length of stay
Significantly fewer stress behaviors and lower cortisol levels, with shorter adoption timelines by approximately four days
No difference in behavioral stress indicators but significantly reduced cortisol
Greater aggression and increased agonistic interactions
mcqs.e: Pair-housed dogs showed fewer stress behaviors (lip licking, whining, ears back), greater cortisol reductions, and shorter adoption timelines (~4 days less), with minimal aggression concerns.

mcqs.q: What physiological measure was used alongside behavioral observation to assess welfare in a shelter dog pair-housing study?
o: Salivary oxytocin concentration
Serum cortisol by venipuncture
Urinary cortisol:creatinine ratio
Fecal glucocorticoid metabolite concentration
mcqs.e: Urine was collected for cortisol:creatinine (UCC) analysis—a non-invasive, practical physiological welfare indicator that confirmed the behavioral finding of reduced stress in pair-housed dogs.

mcqs.q: Which statement best characterizes the welfare implications of compatible pair-housing for shelter dogs, based on this PLoS ONE study?
o: Pair-housing has proximate welfare benefits (reduced stress) but no ultimate benefit (adoption outcomes unchanged)
Pair-housing has both proximate (reduced stress indicators and cortisol) and ultimate welfare benefits (shorter adoption timelines)
Pair-housing is contraindicated due to high rates of aggression between unfamiliar dogs
Pair-housing benefits are limited to puppies under 6 months of age
mcqs.e: The study demonstrated both proximate benefits (reduced behavioral stress and lower cortisol) and ultimate benefits (shorter time to adoption by ~4 days), with minimal aggression.

title: Shelter dog behavior after adoption: Using the C-BARQ to track dog behavior changes through the first six months after adoption
authors: Bohland KR, Lilly ML, Herron ME, Arruda AG, O'Quin JM
abstract: This prospective observational cohort study examined behavioral changes in shelter-adopted dogs during their initial six months in new homes. Ninety-nine dog owners from five Ohio shelters completed surveys using the Canine Behavioral Assessment and Research Questionnaire (C-BARQ) at 7, 30, 90, and 180 days post-adoption. Key findings revealed high prevalence rates for various behaviors, including stranger-directed aggression (81.7%), owner-directed aggression (32.3%), dog-directed aggression (75%) and separation-related behaviors. Over the study period, stranger-directed aggression, excitability, touch sensitivity, training difficulty, and chasing increased, while separation-related behaviors and attachment decreased. Psychotropic medication use in shelters predicted increased stranger-directed aggression post-adoption. Despite these behavioral changes, owners reported high satisfaction levels with their dogs' overall behavior and adjustment.

mcqs.q: In a six-month prospective study tracking C-BARQ scores in 99 shelter-adopted dogs, which behavior INCREASED over time post-adoption?
o: Separation-related behaviors
Owner attachment
Stranger-directed aggression and excitability
Owner-directed aggression
mcqs.e: Stranger-directed aggression, excitability, touch sensitivity, training difficulty, and chasing all increased over the six months, while separation-related behaviors and attachment decreased.

mcqs.q: A prospective cohort study used the C-BARQ to assess post-adoption shelter dog behavior. What was the prevalence of stranger-directed aggression at any point in the first six months?
mcqs.e: 81.7% of dogs showed stranger-directed aggression; 75% showed dog-directed aggression; 32.3% showed owner-directed aggression. High prevalence underscores the importance of post-adoption behavior counseling.

mcqs.q: According to C-BARQ post-adoption tracking in shelter dogs, prior shelter use of psychotropic medications was associated with which outcome?
o: Decreased stranger-directed aggression post-adoption due to improved socialization
Increased stranger-directed aggression post-adoption
No difference in any behavioral domain post-adoption
Improved separation-related behavior scores
mcqs.e: Psychotropic medication use in the shelter setting predicted increased stranger-directed aggression after adoption, a finding relevant to discharge counseling and adopter preparation.

title: The Influence of Brief Outing and Temporary Fostering Programs on Shelter Dog Welfare
authors: Gunter LM, Blade EM, Gilchrist RJ, Nixon BJ, Reed JL, Platzer JM, Wurpts IC, Feuerbacher EN, Wynne CDL
abstract: The research team examined whether brief outings and temporary foster stays improved shelter dog outcomes. Analyzing data from 1,955 dogs receiving interventions and 25,946 control dogs across 51 shelters, they found that brief outings and temporary fostering stays increased dogs' likelihood of adoption by approximately five and fourteen times respectively. While intervention dogs had longer pre-intervention shelter stays, post-intervention stays averaged just 10 days before adoption. Programs performed better with greater community involvement and adequate resources. The authors conclude these interventions represent evidence-based best practices that can positively impact the outcomes of shelter dogs.

mcqs.q: A large multi-shelter study of 51 shelters found that temporary fostering (versus remaining in shelter) increased shelter dogs' likelihood of adoption by approximately:
o: Two times
Five times
Fourteen times
Twenty-five times
mcqs.e: Temporary fostering increased adoption likelihood ~14-fold; brief outings increased it ~5-fold. Both are evidence-based welfare interventions that dramatically improve dog outcomes.

mcqs.q: In the multi-shelter outing/fostering intervention study, what was the average length of shelter stay AFTER the intervention before adoption?
o: 1 day
10 days
30 days
60 days
mcqs.e: Despite longer pre-intervention stays, dogs averaged only 10 days in the shelter post-intervention before adoption, showing rapid conversion once dogs had outing or foster experience.

title: Cat Foster Program Outcomes: Behavior, Stress, and Cat–Human Interaction
authors: Vitale KR, Frank DH, Conroy J, Udell MAR
abstract: The researchers investigated whether placing shelter cats in foster homes—even temporarily—produces stress or behavioral problems. They compared cats placed in overnight or week-long foster care with cats remaining in shelters, measuring stress through cortisol levels and behavioral assessments. Key findings indicate that foster cats did not display decreased social behavior, increased fear or aggression, or increased cortisol levels while in the foster home. Cats experienced litter box aversion on the first night but resumed normal behavior afterward. Foster volunteers engaged in petting, playing, and cuddling activities with their temporary charges. The research demonstrates that short-term fostering appears safe and potentially beneficial, suggesting shelters can use foster programs during overcrowding without harming cat welfare. The authors conclude this information could contribute to life-saving efforts by enabling cats to temporarily leave shelters when space is limited.

mcqs.q: A controlled study comparing shelter cats placed in temporary foster homes to cats remaining in shelters found which of the following regarding foster cat welfare?
o: Foster cats displayed significantly higher cortisol levels and increased aggression
Foster cats showed no increase in fear, aggression, or cortisol, suggesting short-term foster care is safe
Foster cats displayed decreased social behavior indicating stress from environmental change
Foster cats had higher disease transmission rates due to novel pathogen exposure
mcqs.e: Foster cats did not display increased fear, aggression, or cortisol levels; the only transient finding was litter box aversion on the first night, which resolved. The study supports foster programs as welfare-positive.

mcqs.q: What was the only notable behavioral finding during the first night of shelter cat placement in short-term foster care?
o: Increased aggression toward foster caregiver
Elevated cortisol detected in urine samples
Litter box aversion, which resolved with subsequent normal behavior
Reduced social interaction with foster caregivers lasting the full foster period
mcqs.e: The sole transient finding was litter box aversion on the first night; cats resumed normal behavior afterward and showed no persistent welfare compromise.

title: Animal Cruelty in New York City: Cruelty Cases Presented to the ASPCA in Partnership with the NYPD 2013–2022
authors: Caldwell S, Patterson-Kane E, Brandler E, Gupta M, Lockwood R
abstract: The research examined companion animal abuse reports in New York City over a nine-year period (2013–2022). The ASPCA received 2,783 cases involving 5,745 animals through collaboration with the NYPD. The majority involved dogs (82%), followed by cats (15%) and other species (4%). Dogs were most frequently reported for suspected neglect, representing 63% of canine cases. Cats showed a different pattern, with 58% of feline cases involving suspected non-accidental injury. Referral sources included law enforcement (37%), municipal shelters (14%), and veterinarians (11%). The authors concluded that neglect represents a commonly documented form of animal abuse, while cat abuse appears less well understood and may be under-reported or more severe.

mcqs.q: In a nine-year review of ASPCA-NYPD animal cruelty cases in New York City, what was the most common type of abuse documented in canine cases?
o: Non-accidental injury
Neglect
Poisoning
Abandonment
mcqs.e: 63% of dog cases involved suspected neglect, while cats showed a different pattern with 58% involving suspected non-accidental injury—a key distinction for forensic triage.

mcqs.q: In the ASPCA-NYPD cruelty case series (2013–2022), which referral source contributed the highest proportion of animal cruelty cases?
o: Municipal animal shelters (14%)
Veterinarians (11%)
Law enforcement (37%)
General public reporting directly (49%)
mcqs.e: Law enforcement was the largest referral source at 37%, followed by municipal shelters (14%) and veterinarians (11%). This highlights the critical role of inter-agency partnerships in cruelty case identification.

mcqs.q: A 2025 retrospective analysis of NYC animal cruelty cases found that feline cases disproportionately involved suspected non-accidental injury rather than neglect. What percentage of cat cases involved suspected non-accidental injury?
mcqs.e: 58% of feline cases involved suspected non-accidental injury—a stark contrast to dogs (63% neglect). The authors note cat abuse may be under-reported or more severe.

title: Animal Abuse Investigations: Challenges and Recommendations to Improve Animal and Human Welfare
authors: Niemiec R, Kogan LR
abstract: The research explores systemic barriers affecting animal cruelty case management in Colorado through interviews with 24 law enforcement and Bureau of Animal Protection personnel. Researchers identified four primary obstacles: a lack of places to take removed animals and resources to care for them; difficulties collaborating with district attorneys; insufficient training on case procedures; and inadequate investigative staff. The study recommends expanding temporary housing capacity, enhancing professional training, employing specialized investigators and mental health professionals, and potentially amending state statutes. Significantly, the authors advocate implementing a trauma-informed model to address psychological impacts on workers handling these distressing cases, recognizing the interconnected welfare of animals, professionals, and communities.

mcqs.q: Interviews with 24 Colorado law enforcement and animal protection personnel identified which barrier as a primary obstacle in animal cruelty investigations?
o: Lack of public awareness about reporting cruelty
A lack of places to take removed animals and resources to care for them
Excessive veterinary forensic evidence requirements
Absence of state animal cruelty statutes
mcqs.e: The most immediate practical obstacle identified was insufficient housing capacity and resources for animals removed during investigations—a shelter medicine concern directly relevant to cruelty response.

mcqs.q: What novel welfare framework do Niemiec and Kogan (2024) recommend implementing for personnel conducting animal cruelty investigations?
o: A wildlife-centered conservation framework
A trauma-informed model to address psychological impacts on investigators
A purely legal compliance model focused on statute enforcement
A One Health framework focused solely on zoonotic disease risk
mcqs.e: The authors advocate a trauma-informed model recognizing the psychological toll on animal cruelty investigators, acknowledging the interconnected welfare of animals, professionals, and communities.

title: Forensic Death Investigations of Dog Bite Injuries in 31 Cats
authors: Hsiou CL, Hsu CC, Liao PW, Yang FH, Lee AN, Huang WH
abstract: This forensic veterinary study analyzed bite injury patterns in 31 necropsied cats and applied DNA analysis for species identification. Researchers found that puncture wounds, linear or small round contusions/abrasions, and lacerations/avulsions are characteristic bite-related injuries. The examination of 31 cats revealed the most commonly injured regions included the ventral thorax, hindlimbs, shoulder-to-dorsal thorax, back, abdomen, neck, and hip/tail/perineum. Canine mitochondrial DNA was successfully identified in wound swabs and hair samples from broken claws. The study provided an applicable method for canine DNA identification in cats and reference data for future veterinary forensic investigations of dog bite injuries.

mcqs.q: In a forensic necropsy study of 31 cats with suspected dog bite injuries, what molecular technique was used to confirm canine involvement?
o: Nuclear DNA STR profiling of saliva swabs
Canine mitochondrial DNA identification from wound swabs and hair in broken claws
Serological species-specific antibody testing
Scanning electron microscopy of bite mark morphology
mcqs.e: Canine mitochondrial DNA was successfully identified in wound swabs and hair samples from broken claws, providing a forensic species identification method applicable in veterinary cruelty cases.

mcqs.q: Which anatomical regions were most commonly injured in cats with fatal dog bite injuries in this forensic investigation?
o: Head, ears, and orbital region
Ventral thorax, hindlimbs, and shoulder-to-dorsal thorax area
Distal limbs and paw pads exclusively
Abdominal flank only
mcqs.e: The ventral thorax, hindlimbs, and shoulder-to-dorsal thorax were among the most commonly injured regions, with additional involvement of back, abdomen, neck, and hip/tail/perineum.

title: Documenting non-accidental injury patterns in a dog abuse investigation: A collaborative approach between forensic anthropology and veterinary pathology
authors: Bartelink EJ, Clinkinbeard S, Spessard C, Kilmartin A, Spangler WL
abstract: This investigation involved four deceased canines whose remains were excavated from a residential property suspected of animal abuse. Researchers used forensic anthropology and veterinary pathology collaboration to examine skeletonized remains. The analysis revealed evidence of perimortem blunt force trauma on all four skeletons, with injuries concentrated on the axial skeleton and pelvis. One dog exhibited healed rib fractures suggesting previous trauma weeks before death—findings inconsistent with the dog owner's account and instrumental in resolving the case. The study demonstrates how collaboration between forensic anthropologists and veterinary pathologists can effectively document skeletal trauma and non-accidental injury patterns in animal abuse investigations.

mcqs.q: A forensic investigation of four dogs in a suspected animal abuse case found perimortem blunt force trauma on all skeletons. Which additional finding was most significant in refuting the owner's account?
o: Chemical toxicology evidence consistent with antifreeze poisoning
Healed rib fractures indicating previous trauma weeks before death
Absence of any skeletal injuries in one dog
Identical perimortem fracture patterns suggesting simultaneous death
mcqs.e: Healed rib fractures in one dog proved prior traumatic events occurring weeks before death—a chronological finding that directly contradicted the owner's account and was pivotal in resolving the case.

mcqs.q: In this Journal of Forensic Sciences dog abuse case, what was the value of the collaborative approach between forensic anthropologists and veterinary pathologists?
o: Forensic anthropologists provided species identification while veterinary pathologists provided toxicology analysis
Forensic anthropologists contributed expertise in skeletal trauma analysis to complement veterinary pathology findings in documenting non-accidental injuries
The collaboration was primarily administrative, with each discipline working independently
Forensic anthropologists contributed only to fresh tissue examination
mcqs.e: Forensic anthropologists brought skeletal trauma analysis expertise to complement veterinary pathological findings, enabling comprehensive documentation of non-accidental injuries including timing and mechanism.

title: A multidisciplinary investigation of chronic animal abuse: Collaboration between veterinary forensics and forensic anthropology
authors: Smith-Blackmore M, Bethard JD
abstract: The study describes a case involving an injured juvenile female mixed breed dog discovered in an urban area. The animal was deemed to have irreparable injuries and was humanely euthanized. A forensic veterinarian collaborated with a forensic anthropologist to document skeletal trauma sustained before death. The examination revealed numerous injuries in various stages of healing diagnostic of non-accidental injuries. The authors conclude that forensic anthropologists can provide valuable support in analyzing bone remains in veterinary forensic cases involving suspected abuse.

mcqs.q: In a 2021 Journal of Forensic Sciences case report, what skeletal finding in a juvenile dog was diagnostic of chronic non-accidental injury?
o: A single acute perimortem fracture of the femur
Numerous injuries in various stages of healing, indicating repeated traumatic episodes
Pathological fractures consistent with metabolic bone disease
Evidence of a single high-velocity impact to the cranium
mcqs.e: Numerous injuries in various stages of healing are diagnostic of repeated trauma over time—a hallmark of chronic non-accidental injury—as opposed to a single acute traumatic event.

mcqs.q: What role did the forensic anthropologist play in the multidisciplinary animal abuse investigation described by Smith-Blackmore and Bethard (2021)?
o: Performed chemical toxicology screening of tissue samples
Provided expertise in analyzing bone remains to document skeletal trauma
Conducted behavioral assessment of the dog prior to euthanasia
Managed legal documentation and chain of custody
mcqs.e: The forensic anthropologist contributed expertise in skeletal analysis to document bone trauma, complementing the forensic veterinarian's examination—a methodology applicable to cases with skeletonized or badly injured remains.

title: Assessing the Impact of a Virtual Shelter Medicine Rotation on Veterinary Students' Knowledge, Skills, and Attitudes Regarding Access to Veterinary Care
authors: Hoffman CL, Spencer TG, Makolinski KV
abstract: The study examined how incorporating detailed information about veterinary care accessibility within a shelter medicine rotation affected fourth-year veterinary students. Participants engaged in either a control group virtual rotation or an experimental group that included an interactive online module focused on access barriers. Results indicated that all students developed more positive perspectives on nonprofit veterinary clinics and believed veterinarians should offer affordable treatment options. The experimental group specifically showed increased awareness of the potential for implicit bias toward pet owners and demonstrated reduced judgmental tendencies toward clients. These students also reported greater confidence in providing incremental care options. The authors conclude that curriculum emphasizing access to veterinary care enhances students' preparedness to serve diverse clientele through varied treatment and payment approaches.

mcqs.q: In a randomized study comparing a standard virtual shelter medicine rotation to one augmented with an access-to-care module, what was the unique benefit of the augmented curriculum?
o: Greater surgical competency in high-volume sterilization techniques
Increased awareness of implicit bias toward pet owners and greater confidence offering incremental care options
Improved knowledge of pharmacology in shelter settings
Better performance on objective structured clinical examination (OSCE) stations
mcqs.e: The experimental group showed increased awareness of implicit bias toward pet owners, reduced judgment of clients, and greater confidence providing incremental care—attitudinal outcomes not achieved by the standard rotation alone.

mcqs.q: Following a virtual shelter medicine rotation (with or without the access module), what attitude change was observed in ALL student participants?
o: Increased skepticism about the value of nonprofit veterinary clinics
More positive perspectives on nonprofit veterinary clinics and belief that veterinarians should offer affordable treatment options
Decreased interest in working with underserved populations
Increased preference for specialist referral over spectrum-of-care approaches
mcqs.e: All students—including the control group—developed more positive perspectives on nonprofit clinics and agreed veterinarians should offer affordable treatment options, suggesting shelter medicine rotations broadly shift attitudes.

title: Shelter Medicine Programs Support Multiple AAVMC Competency Domains: A Survey of Shelter Medicine Programming at AVMA-Accredited Colleges
authors: Dalrymple AM, DeTar LG, Weisent J, Kreisler RE
abstract: This study evaluated shelter medicine education availability at 54 AVMA-accredited veterinary colleges. Researchers distributed a 24-question survey from July–September 2023, receiving 43 responses (80% response rate). Results showed 88% of institutions offered formal shelter medicine coursework, with programs typically established around 2012. The survey found colleges employed 118 shelter medicine instructors (median of 2 per institution), though only 5% held tenure positions. Notably, 21% of responding schools had discontinued their programs, primarily due to lack of faculty and lack of a relationship with a shelter. The median program addressed 7 of 9 AAVMC competency domains, with many institutions addressing all 9 domains. The study highlights both the breadth of shelter medicine education and its vulnerability due to precarious faculty appointment structures.

mcqs.q: A 2023 survey of AVMA-accredited veterinary colleges found what percentage offered formal shelter medicine coursework, and what was the median number of AAVMC competency domains addressed?
o: 65% offered courses, median 4 of 9 domains
88% offered courses, median 7 of 9 domains
95% offered courses, median 9 of 9 domains
72% offered courses, median 5 of 9 domains
mcqs.e: 88% of responding institutions offered formal shelter medicine coursework, and the median number of AAVMC competency domains addressed was 7 of 9, with many schools addressing all 9.

mcqs.q: In a survey of AVMA-accredited colleges' shelter medicine programs, what was the primary reason institutions gave for DISCONTINUING their shelter medicine programs?
o: Lack of student interest and poor enrollment
Lack of faculty and/or lack of a relationship with a shelter
Budget cuts to clinical programs overall
Accreditation requirement changes eliminating shelter medicine
mcqs.e: 21% of schools had discontinued programs; the primary reasons were lack of faculty and lack of a shelter relationship—highlighting the structural fragility of shelter medicine education.

mcqs.q: What faculty appointment characteristic was identified as a vulnerability for shelter medicine programs in AVMA-accredited veterinary colleges?
o: Most shelter medicine faculty held tenure, limiting program flexibility
Only 5% of shelter medicine instructors held tenure positions, indicating precarious employment
Shelter medicine was exclusively taught by adjunct instructors with no faculty appointments
Shelter medicine programs lacked any dedicated faculty and relied on volunteer clinicians
mcqs.e: Only 5% of shelter medicine instructors held tenure positions, meaning most programs depended on non-tenured faculty whose positions are more vulnerable to elimination—a systemic risk to the field.

title: Veterinary Student Skills Learned at an Access to Care Clinic: Beyond Medicine and Surgery
authors: Alvarez EE, Schultz K, Lygo-Baker S, Chun R
abstract: The research examined how a two-week rotation at Wisconsin Companion Animal Resources, Education, and Social Services (WisCARES) affected veterinary student development. Of 97 respondents with background information, 70% had minimal experience serving diverse or low-income populations beforehand. Students reported significant improvements post-rotation: increased comfort levels and compassion when working with low-income or homeless pet owners (mean = 4.54 and 4.42 respectively), greater ease interacting with members of different race or ethnicity groups (mean = 4.21), and enhanced appreciation for human-animal bonds (mean = 4.42). The clinic experience positively influenced clinical confidence, financial communication abilities, and creative case management. Researchers concluded that providing students opportunities to lead cases with economically disadvantaged and racially diverse clientele strengthens their professional readiness and clinical self-assurance.

mcqs.q: In a study of veterinary students rotating at an access-to-care clinic (WisCARES), what percentage of students had minimal prior experience serving diverse or low-income populations before the rotation?
mcqs.e: 70% of respondents had minimal experience serving diverse or low-income populations before the rotation, highlighting the access-to-care clinic as a gap-filling educational experience.

mcqs.q: Beyond clinical medicine and surgery skills, a two-week access-to-care rotation at WisCARES improved which student competencies?
o: Surgical speed and instrument handling
Financial communication, comfort working with diverse populations, and appreciation for human-animal bonds
Radiograph interpretation and emergency triage
Research methodology and evidence-based medicine skills
mcqs.e: The rotation improved financial communication, comfort and compassion with low-income/homeless clients, cultural competence with diverse populations, and appreciation for the human-animal bond—non-surgical professional skills.

title: Evaluation of a Student-Led Community-Based Veterinary Clinic for Disabled Low-Income Clients: A Case Study of the University of Florida PAWS Program
authors: Otero DK, James TG, Stone AE
abstract: The study evaluated a student-led veterinary clinic serving disabled individuals with low incomes (the PAWS Program at the University of Florida). During 2020–2021, the program conducted 162 monthly appointments with approximately 15 veterinary students volunteering per clinic session. Key findings: clients attributed enrollment in the clinic with improved quality-of-life and reduction of financial burden, saving clients roughly $2,050 per pet annually. Students demonstrated positive attitude changes and increased readiness to provide care to people with disabilities and people experiencing low socioeconomic position. The clinic effectively facilitated core curriculum learning outcomes while addressing intersectional inequities in veterinary care access, underscoring the value of community health practice within veterinary education.

mcqs.q: The University of Florida PAWS program, a student-led clinic serving disabled low-income clients, reduced the annual veterinary cost burden for enrolled clients by approximately how much per pet?
mcqs.e: Clients saved roughly $2,050 per pet annually through the PAWS clinic, demonstrating the concrete financial impact of access-to-care educational programs.

mcqs.q: A case study of the UF PAWS veterinary clinic identified which dual benefit of community-based, student-led access-to-care programs?
o: Improved faculty research productivity and departmental revenue generation
Improved client quality of life and financial burden reduction, alongside positive student attitude changes toward serving underserved populations
Increased student surgical volume without educational outcome improvements
Enhanced shelter intake efficiency and disease surveillance
mcqs.e: The program achieved both client-facing outcomes (improved quality of life, reduced financial burden) and student-facing outcomes (positive attitudes toward serving disabled/low-income clients), demonstrating dual value.

title: Cultural Competence Is Everyone's Business: Embedding Cultural Competence in Curriculum Frameworks to Advance Veterinary Education
authors: Gongora J, van Gelderen I, Vost M, Zaki S, Sutherland S, Pye M, Quain A, Taylor R
abstract: The authors describe implementing a curriculum framework at the University of Sydney veterinary program that integrates cultural competence throughout veterinary education. As stated in the article, veterinarians work with culturally and linguistically diverse teams, clients, and communities. The framework encompasses defining cultural competence, perceptions of animals, effective communication, and community engagement in a range of contexts. Learning outcomes were aligned with course objectives and institutional graduate qualities. The approach employed constructive alignment by connecting outcomes to teaching activities and assessment, with vertical integration across the curriculum. The integration aligns with accreditation recommendations and evidence-based practices in medicine, nursing, and allied health disciplines.

mcqs.q: The University of Sydney's cultural competence curriculum framework for veterinary education used which pedagogical approach to embed cultural competence throughout the program?
o: Single stand-alone elective module in final year
Constructive alignment linking cultural competence outcomes to teaching activities, assessment, and vertical integration across the curriculum
Mandatory extramural placement at culturally diverse clinics in second year only
Online self-directed modules with no formal assessment component
mcqs.e: The framework used constructive alignment—linking defined outcomes to teaching activities and assessment—with vertical integration across the curriculum, consistent with accreditation standards and allied health models.

mcqs.q: According to Gongora et al. (2023), which factor was most critical to sustaining the cultural competence curriculum framework once implemented?
o: Student demand and positive course evaluations
Staff engagement and stakeholder involvement
External accreditation body mandates
Faculty tenure status and research output
mcqs.e: The authors emphasized that staff engagement and stakeholder involvement were essential to sustaining the curriculum changes—without buy-in from faculty and stakeholders, the framework would not be maintained.

title: Evaluation of Population Management Based on Trap–Neuter–Return and Trap–Neuter–Adoption Practices in a Free-Roaming Cat Colony in the Federal District, Brazil
authors: Junqueira ANN, Galera PD
abstract: This study evaluated the use of trap-neuter-return (TNR) and trap-neuter-adoption (TNA) in a free-roaming cat colony in Brazil's Federal District over 18 months involving 157 cats that had not previously been managed. The study had three phases: recognition and preparation, TNR/TNA intervention, and monitoring. Following interventions, there was a 47.8% reduction in colony size, and 98.8% of the animals were sterilized. Adoption played an important role in reducing population growth, preventing kitten birth, fostering stronger bonds between caregivers and animals, and protecting against death, disappearance, and abandonment. The study demonstrates that combining TNR with adoption (TNA) provides complementary population management benefits beyond sterilization alone.

mcqs.q: In an 18-month TNR and TNA intervention study involving 157 previously unmanaged cats in Brazil, what was the overall colony size reduction achieved?
mcqs.e: The colony size was reduced by 47.8% over 18 months, with 98.8% sterilization coverage. Combining TNR with adoption (TNA) provided additional reductions beyond sterilization effects alone.

mcqs.q: What was the unique contribution of the Trap-Neuter-Adoption (TNA) component compared to TNR alone in this Brazilian community cat study?
o: TNA was less effective than TNR alone at reducing colony size
TNA reduced population while also preventing kitten birth, fostering caregiver-cat bonds, and protecting against death and abandonment
TNA was only beneficial for kittens under 8 weeks of age
TNA increased caregiver burden without measurable population impact
mcqs.e: TNA complemented TNR by removing individuals from the colony through adoption, preventing kitten births, strengthening caregiver bonds, and reducing losses to death, disappearance, and abandonment.

title: Four Years of Promising Trap-Neuter-Return (TNR) in Córdoba, Spain: A Scalable Model for Urban Feline Management
authors: Luzardo OP, Vara-Rascón M, Dufau A, Infante E, Travieso-Aja MM
abstract: The research documents Córdoba's citywide TNR initiative involving 225 groups of cats (usually named colonies) managed from 2020 onward. The program achieved 95% sterilization coverage while limiting population growth despite external pressures like abandonment and immigration from unmanaged areas. Key findings indicate an overall population decline of 2.68%, though modeling suggests this prevented approximately 70% population growth that would have occurred without intervention. Program costs averaged EUR 0.62 annually per resident. Population viability analysis projects a potential 55% reduction by 2028 with sustained implementation. The study emphasizes the initiative's integration of citizen science and adaptive management as a replicable framework for large-scale TNR initiatives in urban contexts addressing animal welfare, public health, and biodiversity conservation concerns.

mcqs.q: A four-year citywide TNR program in Córdoba, Spain achieved 95% sterilization coverage. Despite only a 2.68% actual population decline, what was the modeling-projected impact of the program?
o: The program prevented approximately 30% population growth that would otherwise have occurred
The program prevented approximately 70% population growth that would otherwise have occurred
The program accelerated population growth by drawing in unsterilized immigration
The population would have declined 70% even without the intervention
mcqs.e: The actual colony size declined only 2.68%, but modeling showed the program prevented ~70% growth that would have occurred without intervention—demonstrating that apparent small declines mask a large preventive effect.

mcqs.q: Population viability analysis from the Córdoba citywide TNR program projects what outcome if the program is sustained through 2028?
o: Complete eradication of all free-roaming cats by 2028
A potential 55% reduction in the free-roaming cat population by 2028
Population stabilization at current levels with no further reduction
Population increase due to immigration overwhelming sterilization rates
mcqs.e: The viability analysis projects a 55% reduction by 2028 with sustained implementation, illustrating the long-term cumulative benefit of consistent large-scale TNR programs.
